deep.reconstruction:
Context. This sheet belongs to Riemann's heat-conduction notes. The previous and next pages ask when a second-order operator Δ' (e.g. ∂α∂β + e∂α + f∂β) is compatible with the heat operator Δ − ∂t (e.g. a∂α² + b∂β² + c∂α + d∂β). Compatible means that the side condition Δ'u = 0 is preserved by the heat flow. The test is that the commutator ΔΔ' − Δ'Δ vanishes, at least modulo Δ'. This page has four blocks.

(A) Top left: variational setup and adapted coordinates.
- Several lines are crossed out.
- He writes the anisotropic Dirichlet integral δ∬(a u_x² + 2b u_x u_y + c u_y²) dx dy = 0. Its Euler–Lagrange equation is (a u_x + b u_y)_x + (b u_x + c u_y)_y = 0, the stationary anisotropic conduction equation of the 1861 Paris memoir.
- He considers two directional derivatives, α u_x + β u_y and α' u_x + β' u_y = q ∂u/∂s1.
- He introduces curvilinear coordinates through integrating factors: β dx − α dy = m ds1 and β' dx − α' dy = m' ds2. Hence α ∂s1/∂x + β ∂s1/∂y = 0, so the field α∂x + β∂y differentiates along the level lines of s1.
- He then states the programme:
  - Δu = ∂u/∂t and Δ'u = 0, with condition (ΔΔ' − Δ'Δ)u = 0.
  - In coordinates s2, s3 the operator Δ' is reduced to the hyperbolic normal form ∂²u/∂s2∂s3 + α ∂u/∂s2 (+…) = 0.
- He integrates once in s2, taking m ∂u/∂s3 as the s2-primitive:
  m u_{s3} = −∫α u_{s2} ds2 = −uα + ∫u α_{s2} ds2 (integration by parts).
- He tries the substitution u_{s3} = m p, u_{s2} = n p_{s2}.
  - Equality of mixed derivatives gives (mp)_{s2} = n_{s3} p_{s2} + n p_{s2 s3}.
  - Dividing by n and integrating in s2: ∫[(1/n)(mp)_{s2} − (log n)_{s3} p_{s2}] ds2 = p_{s3}.
  - He begins integrating by parts: (1/n) m p − (log n)_{s3} p − ∫…. This is left unfinished.

(B) Middle left: secular (Jordan-chain) solutions of the heat equation.
- If Δv = μv and Δu = μu + v (Δ the 3-D Laplacian), then w = e^{μt}(t v + u) satisfies Δw = ∂w/∂t.
- Check (mine): w_t = e^{μt}(μ t v + μ u + v) and Δw = e^{μt}(t μ v + μ u + v). These agree.

(C) Right column: commutator of the Laplacian with a general second-order operator.
- The heat equation Δu = u_t is written first.
- For L = Σ a_{ιι'} ∂ι∂ι' + Σ b_ι ∂ι, he notes that L Δu = 0 has the same form as Lu = 0. The leading obstruction in ΔL − LΔ is Σ 2 ∂a_{ιι'}/∂x_{ι''} ∂³u/∂xι∂xι'∂xι''.
- He specializes to Δ = ∂x² + δ with δ = ∂y² + ∂z², and L = ∂x² + θ∂x + η. Here θ, η are operators in y, z whose coefficients depend on x, y, z.
- He expands ΔLu − LΔu (or its negative) term by term:
  θ_xx u_x + 2θ_x u_xx + 2η_x u_x + η_xx u + (δθ − θδ) u_x + (δη − ηδ) u.
- He eliminates u_xx using Lu = 0, i.e. u_xx = −θu_x − ηu, so 2θ_x u_xx → −2θ_x∘θ u_x − 2θ_x∘η u.
- Collecting the coefficients of u_x and u gives the two operator identities on the page:
  - (I) θδ − δθ − θ_xx − 2η_x + 2θ_x θ = 0
  - (II) ηδ − δη − η_xx + 2θ_x η = 0
  I re-derived these and they are correct, with operator products read as compositions.
- Ansatz: θ = a∂y + b∂z + c, for which θδ − δθ = −2(∂θ/∂y)∂y − 2(∂θ/∂z)∂z − (δ-coefficients). He jots −2(∂η/∂y)∂y − ∂²η/∂y² for the analogous commutator with η.

(D) Bottom right: the 2-D case.
- He restricts to two variables: Δ = ∂x² + ∂y², δ = ∂y², θ = a∂y + …, η = p∂y² + ….
- Top-order coefficients:
  - ∂y³ in (II): [p∂y², ∂y²] = −2p_y∂y³ and 2a_x∂y∘p∂y² = 2a_x p∂y³. Hence −2p_y + 2a_x p = 0, i.e. a_x = (log p)_y.
  - ∂y² in (I): −2a_y − 2p_x + 2a a_x = 0.
- First potential attempt: a = m_y, log p = m_x. This would give e^{m_x} m_xx = m_y m_xy − m_yy; the attempt is crossed out.
- Second potential: write (I) as ∂x(p − a²/2) = −∂y a. Then p − ½a² = m_y, a = −m_x, so p = m_y + ½ m_x².
- Substituting into a_x = (log p)_y gives a single nonlinear PDE for m:
  m_yy + m_x m_xy + m_y m_xx + ½ m_x² m_xx = 0.
  This is the line written as m_yy + m_x m_xy = −m_xx m_y − ½ m_x² m_xx.
- The aim is to classify second-order operators compatible with (commuting modulo itself with) the Laplacian/heat operator. Such operators single out special coordinate systems in which the heat equation reduces.
errors: Block A: the reduced normal form line is garbled ('∂²u/∂s3∂s2 + α∂u/∂s2 + ∂²u/∂s2∂s3'). The mixed derivative is duplicated; the second term is presumably a first-order term in s3. Not a substantive error.
Block A: the integration over s2 in the p-substitution is left unfinished; no constants or functions of s3 of integration are written.

Block C: the side note for the η-commutator reads −2(∂η/∂y)∂y − 2∂²η/∂y² in the transcription. The correct expansion of [η, ∂y²] has −2η_y∂y − η_yy (coefficient 1 on the second term). Either a slip or a mis-transcription.
Block C: θδ − δθ = −2(∂θ/∂y)∂y − 2(∂θ/∂z)∂z omits the zeroth-order term −(δθ)(coefficients). This is harmless at top order, which is all he uses.
Block D: the transcribed 'a = 2∂m/∂x' is inconsistent with p = m_y + ½m_x² and p − ½a² = m_y. The consistent choice is a = −∂m/∂x, so it is likely a misreading or slip.
Block D: in the final PDE for m the term ½ m_x² m_xx must carry a minus sign on the right-hand side, i.e. the same sign as −m_xx m_y. A '+' as transcribed would be wrong.
Block D: the first potential choice (a = m_y, log p = m_x) is abandoned in favour of the second; the crossed-out line belongs to that abandoned route.

results.what: Euler–Lagrange equation of the anisotropic Dirichlet integral ∬(a u_x² + 2b u_x u_y + c u_y²), and coordinates adapted to vector fields via integrating factors (β dx − α dy = m ds1)
results.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange equation for a quadratic form; straightening of vector fields / characteristic coordinates
results.usually_credited_to: Euler/Lagrange; Gauss/Jacobi for integrating-factor coordinates; Riemann's own 1861 Paris memoir for the anisotropic heat setting

results.what: Partial integration of the normal form u_{s2s3} + α u_{s2} = 0 and the substitution u_{s3} = m p, u_{s2} = n p_{s2}
results.modern_name: Integration of hyperbolic normal forms (precursor of Laplace cascade / Riemann's method)
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace (cascade method), Riemann 1860 for the hyperbolic theory

results.what: Secular solutions e^{μt}(t v + u) of the heat equation built from a Jordan chain Δv = μv, Δu = μu + v
results.modern_name: Generalized eigenfunction (Jordan block) solutions of u_t = Δu
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Lagrange/Cauchy for ODE systems with repeated roots)

results.what: Conditions for a second-order operator L = ∂x² + θ∂x + η to commute with the Laplacian modulo L: θδ − δθ − θ_xx − 2η_x + 2θ_xθ = 0 and ηδ − δη − η_xx + 2θ_xη = 0
results.modern_name: Compatibility / (conditional) symmetry operators of Laplace and heat equations; second-order commuting operators and separation of variables
results.usually_credited_to: Lie (1881) for symmetries of the heat equation; Eisenhart (1934) and Miller, Kalnins (1970s) for second-order symmetry operators and separability

results.what: 2-D top-order conditions a_x = (log p)_y and ∂x(p − a²/2) = −a_y, solved by a potential m giving m_yy + m_x m_xy + m_y m_xx + ½ m_x² m_xx = 0
results.modern_name: Reduction of the compatibility system to a single nonlinear PDE via a potential

deep.surprise_reason: The page has two notable features. Riemann systematically looks for second-order operators compatible with (commuting with, modulo the operator) the Laplacian/heat operator. He also derives correct operator-valued commutation conditions. This anticipates in spirit the later theory of symmetry operators and separability (Lie, Eisenhart, Miller). However, it is exploratory, incomplete, and grows naturally out of his 1861 work on transforming the heat equation. The calculations themselves are routine, so this is a notable unpublished detail rather than a major priority result.

transcription_corrections: 'e^{μt} t v + u' should read e^{μt}(t v + u).
'θ=(a∂_y+b∂_z+c)∂_y²+∂_z²' is most likely two separate items: θ = a∂y + b∂z + c, with δ = ∂y² + ∂z² recalled alongside.
'a = 2∂m/∂x' (last line) is probably a = −∂m/∂x, the only reading consistent with p − ½a² = m_y and p = m_y + ½m_x².
In the long m-equation the coefficient '+½(∂m/∂x)² ∂²m/∂x²' should be −½(∂m/∂x)² ∂²m/∂x² on the right side; the remainder of that line is crossed out.
'ds/dx α + ∂s1/∂y β = 0' should be ∂s1/∂x α + ∂s1/∂y β = 0.
'∂²u/∂s3² = α∂′' is an unfinished or illegible fragment, not a formula.
The side note '−2∂η/∂y ∂y − 2∂²η/∂y²' may be −2(∂η/∂y)∂y − ∂²η/∂y² in the image; the latter is mathematically correct.
